questions.q: Ada is logged in with a valid token and tries to delete Linus's task. The permission engine says no. Which status should the API answer?
questions.explain: 401 means "I don't know who you are" (authentication failed). The server knows this is Ada; the answer to what she asked is no, so it is 403.

questions.q: What is a privilege escalation?
questions.explain: Authorization bugs that let someone do more than they should are among the most common serious security bugs in real APIs. Much of the lesson shows such attacks and how they are refused.
options: A user who forgot their password
A normal user who manages to act as an admin, or to edit other people's data
An admin who logs in twice
A request that takes too long

questions.q: In role-based access control (RBAC), how do users get their rights?
questions.explain: Roles keep rights manageable: change the member role once and every member changes with it.
options: Each right is given to each person, one by one
Rights are given to a few roles, like member and admin, and each user gets one or more roles
Every user gets every right, and some are taken away
The client sends the rights it needs with each request

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A member inherits task:read from viewer but has no task:delete. Grace's task:* covers delete, but no role grants user:delete, so even an admin is refused: anything not granted is denied.

questions.q: No role grants user:delete. What does engine.can(admin, "user:delete") answer?
questions.explain: An authorization system should always deny by default. "Admin" is just a name; it gets exactly what its permissions say.
options: false: anything no role grants is refused

questions.q: Why must you write await engine.can(actor, "task:read")?
questions.explain: A forgotten await is dangerous: if (engine.can(...)) tests a Promise object, which is truthy, so everyone would be allowed.
options: Because it sends a request to a permission server
It is async, because some checks load data; without await you get a Promise, which is always truthy
Because it is slow on purpose
You don't: can returns a boolean directly

questions.q: Add an editor role between member and admin. Editors can do everything a member can and can update any task, but must not delete tasks. Admin should inherit from editor. The program prints a small table.
questions.explain: Give the editor the one exact permission it needs, task:update, not task:*, which would include delete. inherits brings in everything a member can do.
questions.expected:
member false false
editor true false
admin true true

questions.q: Someone wanted members to "read everything they need" and wrote *:read. What does this print?
questions.explain: *:read means "read on every resource": users, the audit log, anything added later. Nothing failed and nothing was logged. List what the role needs, task:read, instead.

questions.q: Next month you add a user:export action. Which roles get it on day one without anyone deciding so?
questions.explain: A wildcard grants permissions that do not exist yet. Review wildcard grants whenever you add a new action.
options: None: new actions must be granted explicitly
Every role holding a matching wildcard, such as user:* or *:*

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: billing.*:read matches billing:read and every billing.something:read. It does not cover other actions, and billingx is a different resource.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Patterns that could never match are refused when the engine is created, even a trailing space. *:* is a valid (if very broad) grant. Failing loudly at startup beats a rule that silently never works.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: check gives the whole decision. reason is machine-readable, for your logs. publicReason, "Access denied", is the only one safe to send to the client.
options:
true role_permission
false no_matching_rule Access denied

true undefined
false Access denied undefined

true role_permission
false forbidden Access denied

questions.q: A request is refused. What should the response body contain?
questions.explain: Internal reasons and explain steps name your rules and policies, which tells an attacker how your system works. Keep them in your logs.
options: The decision's reason, such as rule_deny, and the rule's name
The full explain steps, so the user can fix it
The list of the user's roles

questions.q: The database says Sam's role is "Admin", with a capital A. What does this print?
questions.explain: Role names are compared exactly: "Admin" is not "admin". An unknown role gives nothing, and the engine reports it through onError so you can fix the data. Every failure denies.

questions.q: Why can't roles alone say "a member may edit their own tasks"?
questions.explain: Attribute-based access control (ABAC) rules look at the actor and the resource. isOwner("userId") compares the task's userId with the actor's id.
options: Because roles cannot hold the update action
The answer depends on the task (who owns it), not only on the user; that needs a rule that looks at the resource (ABAC)
Because ownership is checked by the database

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Ada may update her own task, not Linus's. Without a task, the owner rule has nothing to compare, so it does not apply and she is refused: the safe choice. Grace passes through task:*.

questions.q: Where should the task object you pass to engine.can(actor, "task:update", task) come from?
questions.explain: If the task came from the body, the client would simply write its own id into userId and pass the owner check.
options: From the request body, which contains the task being edited
From your database, loaded by the id in the URL, before the check

questions.q: Members may read tasks, and may update and delete only their own. The Task API stores the owner in userId. Add the missing rule to the member role, using isOwner.
questions.explain: An allow rule on task for ["update", "delete"] with isOwner("userId"). Test both directions: the owner is allowed, someone else is refused.

questions.q: Linus owns task 3. The attacker is user "3". What does this print?
questions.explain: isOwner("id") compares the task's id with the user's id. Task 3 and user "3" match, so the attacker deletes Linus's task. The right field, userId, refuses it. (isOwner treats the number 3 and the string "3" as the same id.)

questions.q: Tasks store their owner in userId, and a rule uses isOwner() with no argument, which reads ownerId. What happens?
questions.explain: Getting the field wrong can fail either way: "id" lets attackers in, a missing field locks everyone out. That is why you test both the owner and a stranger.
options: Every member can delete every task
It is safe but useless: a missing owner never matches, so even the real owner is refused

questions.q: The database stores userId as the number 7; the token gives the id as the string "7". What does this print?
questions.explain: isOwner treats 7 and "7" as the same id on purpose, because database ids are often numbers and token ids strings. A task with no owner never matches.

questions.q: Tasks belong to teams. An old task has no teamId, and the request carries no team either. What does this print?
questions.explain: The hand-written condition compares undefined === undefined, which is true, so a user with no team reads every task without one. The built-in tenantIsolation denies when either side is missing. Missing data must mean no.

questions.q: Write sameTeam, a condition that allows only when the task's teamId and the request's teamId (from ctx.metadata?.get("teamId")) are both non-empty strings and equal. Missing data must mean no.
questions.explain: Check that both values exist before you compare them. Otherwise undefined === undefined lets anyone with no team read everything without one.

questions.q: A team condition reads teamId from the check's metadata. Where must that value come from?
questions.explain: If the team came from a header or the query string, an attacker would simply send the task's team and pass.
options: Something the client cannot choose: the verified token or your database

questions.q: A deny rule protects locked tasks. What does this print?
questions.explain: A deny rule beats even an admin's task:*, but only for the actions it names, so reading is still fine. With no task, the condition throws; the engine cannot tell whether the task is locked, so it applies the deny rule (fails closed) and reports the error.
options:
true
false
true
reported by RuleCondition.locked-tasks
false

true
false
false
reported by RuleCondition.locked-tasks
true

questions.q: An allow rule's condition throws. What does this print?
questions.explain: An allow rule whose condition throws simply does not apply. A deny rule whose condition throws applies. Either way, an error can only make the answer "no".
options:
true
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined

questions.q: A role grants task:update, and a deny rule for task:update applies. What is the answer, and why?
questions.explain: With deny-overrides, grants add up but one applying deny takes access away. That makes deny rules the right tool for restrictions.
options: Allowed, because the role grant came first
Denied: by default the engine uses deny-overrides, so any applying deny rule wins over every grant
It depends on the order of the rules
The engine throws because the rules conflict

questions.q: The member role grants task:read, so an allow rule would change nothing. Team isolation is enforced with a deny rule instead. What does this print?
questions.explain: not(tenantIsolation(...)) is true whenever the teams differ or a team is missing, so the deny rule applies then. Only a matching team gets through the grant.

questions.q: Members are granted task:read and task:update. Add an engine-wide deny rule named same-team for task, actions read and update, that applies when the actor's team (metadata teamId) and the task's teamId do not match or are missing. Use not and tenantIsolation.
questions.explain: When a role already grants the permission, an allow rule adds nothing. A deny rule takes access away whenever the teams differ or are missing, and deny rules beat every grant.

questions.q: A careless handler builds the actor with the request body spread into it. What does this print?
questions.explain: With the spread, Ada sends "roles": ["admin"] and becomes an admin, or "id": "linus" and becomes the owner. The engine was correct both times; it was given a lie. The secure actor takes the id from the token and the roles from the database.

questions.q: Finish actorFor(tokenUserId, body). Build the actor with createPermissionActor: the id from tokenUserId (the verified token), the roles from rolesInDatabase (an empty list for an unknown user). Ignore the body completely.
questions.explain: The actor's id comes only from the verified token, its roles only from your database. An unknown user gets no roles, so nothing is granted. The body never decides who the caller is.

questions.q: How should an admin change a user's role?
questions.explain: A role, roles, userId or isAdmin field is never on the list of fields a normal update accepts. Changing roles is a separate, admin-only action.
options: Any user may send "roles" in their profile update
Through its own endpoint, protected by its own permission such as user:update-role, that only admins have
By editing the JWT in the browser
Through a hidden isAdmin field in the task update body

questions.q: You need the restriction "tasks can only be changed during office hours". How does the lesson say to write it?
questions.explain: A restriction must never be able to grant access by itself. A deny rule can only say no, so it cannot accidentally let in someone no role allowed.
options: As a deny rule that applies outside office hours, which can only ever take access away
As a check in the client

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The guest has no role, so the deny rule gives it nothing. Ada may delete her own task at 10:00 but not at 20:00. With no hour at all, the condition says "deny": missing data means no.

questions.q: Finish outsideOfficeHours, the condition of a deny rule. Read hour from ctx.metadata?.get("hour"). Return true (deny) when the hour is not a number, or is before 9, or is 17 or later.
questions.explain: The check starts with "is it a number?", so a missing hour or the text "10" is denied. The hour comes from your server's clock, never from the client.
questions.expected:
false true true false
false false

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: None of Ada's two granted permissions is task:delete, but the own-tasks rule applied because she owns the task. Naming your rules pays off: the trace tells you which one decided.
options:
true
yes role Role: member
no  permission No permission matched "task:delete" among 2 granted
yes rule Rule allow: own-tasks
yes permission Decision: allow (role_permission)

true
yes role Role: member
yes permission task:delete
yes permission Decision: allow (role_permission)

false
yes role Role: member
no  permission No permission matched "task:delete" among 2 granted
no  deny Decision: deny (no_matching_rule)

questions.q: Where do explain results belong?
questions.explain: The steps describe your roles and rules. Sent to a client, they would give an attacker a map of your authorization system.
options: In the 403 response, so users understand the refusal
In your logs and debugging; never send the steps to a client
In the database, instead of roles

questions.q: A route that deletes a task does three things. Which order does the lesson use?
questions.explain: Authenticating first means an anonymous caller cannot even learn which task ids exist. The task must be loaded before the check, because the owner rule needs it.
options: Authenticate (401) → load the task by the URL id (404) → authorize this user for this task (403)
Authenticate → authorize without the task → load the task

questions.q: Finish deleteTask(userId, taskId), the core of a DELETE /tasks/:id handler. Return { status: 401 } when userId is missing, { status: 404 } when the task does not exist, { status: 403, error: decision.publicReason } when engine.check refuses, and otherwise delete it and return { status: 200, deleted: id }. Roles come from userRoles.
questions.explain: Authenticate, load, then authorize. Only the publicReason goes back to the client. Ada may delete her own task; Grace, an admin, may delete Linus's.

questions.q: A teammate lets support staff read any task with the condition (ctx) => ctx.metadata?.get("support") === true, filled from request.getHeader("x-support") === "yes". What is wrong?
questions.explain: Anything the client sends can be forged. Who is support staff is a fact your database knows, so it belongs in the actor's roles.
options: Nothing: only support staff know the header
Anyone can send x-support: yes and read every task; make support a role stored in your database and grant it task:read
The header should be X-Support with capitals
It should use the query string instead

questions.q: A locked task must stop members, but an admin can still update it. Finish the deny rule's condition with allOf and not: it applies when the task is locked and the actor is not an admin.
questions.explain: allOf(isLocked, not(isAdmin)) applies only when both are true. isAdmin reads roles your server built from the database, so it is safe to trust.

questions.q: A role grants task:read. You add an allow rule "same team only" for task:read. Does the rule stop team red from reading blue tasks?
questions.explain: An allow rule can only add access. To take access away from something a role grants, you need a deny rule, such as not(tenantIsolation("teamId", "teamId")).
options: Yes, the rule narrows the grant
No: grants add up, so the role's task:read alone already allows it; enforce the team with a deny rule
Yes, rules always run before grants
The engine throws because they overlap

questions.explain: Roles come from the database. A user with no roles gets nothing, and nobody here was granted task:delete.
